entry: Pakistani education activist and film producer. Yousafzai campaigned for girls' schooling in Swat, where the Pakistani [[Taliban]] had at times banned girls from attending school. Shot in the head by a Taliban gunman in 2012, she survived and became a prominent advocate for education. She shared the 2014 Nobel Peace Prize with Kailash Satyarthi, becoming the youngest laureate at 17. She co-authored the international best seller *I Am Malala* (2013). Some critics in Pakistan, including officials, have questioned her account or portrayed her as serving foreign interests.

Landlocked city in East Java, [[Indonesia]] (pop., 2020: 843,810), historically known as Tumapel. Its history dates to the age of the Singhasari Kingdom, and it keeps relics from the Kanjuruhan Kingdom through the Dutch period. Its mild climate made it a popular destination for European residents during Dutch colonization, and it remains popular with international tourists. Dutch-era buildings such as the Kayutangan church and Ijen Cathedral use [[Gothic architecture]]. The city is known as an educational center, and Brawijaya University and Malang State University are among the best universities in Indonesia. Malang is the third-largest city by economy in East Java, after [[Surabaya]] and Kediri. Its population is mostly Javanese, with Madurese and Chinese or Peranakan communities.

Landlocked country in southeastern Africa, bordered by Zambia, Tanzania and Mozambique (pop., 2025: 22,224,282). Its capital and largest city is [[Lilongwe]]. The area was settled around the 10th century by the Akafula, later displaced by Bantu groups who formed kingdoms such as the Maravi. The missionary [[David Livingstone]] reached [[Lake Malawi]] in 1859, and the British designated the territory a protectorate in 1891, renamed Nyasaland in 1907. Nyasaland became independent in 1964 under Prime Minister [[Hastings Banda]] and was renamed Malawi. Banda ruled as a one-party president from 1966 and as president for life from 1971, until multi-party politics was introduced in 1993. He lost the 1994 general election, and power has since passed peacefully. The country is one of the world's least developed, with an economy reliant on agriculture and [[Tobacco]] exports. [[HIV/AIDS]] is highly prevalent.

Archipelago between [[Mainland Southeast Asia]] and Australia, also called *Insulindia* or the Indo-Australian Archipelago. It has been called the Malay world, *Nusantara* and the East Indies over time. The name derives from a 19th-century European concept of a Malay race, and it is controversial in [[Indonesia]] because of its ethnic and colonial connotations. The archipelago includes over 25,000 islands and islets, making it the largest archipelago by area and fifth by number of islands in the world. Its countries include [[Brunei]], East Timor, Indonesia, East Malaysia, [[Papua New Guinea]], the [[Philippines]] and [[Singapore]]. [[Alfred Russel Wallace]] used the term as the title of his influential book *The Malay Archipelago*.

Peninsula in [[Mainland Southeast Asia]], ending at Tanjung Piai, the southernmost point of the Asian continental mainland. It contains [[Malaysia|Peninsular Malaysia]], southern [[Thailand]] and the southern tip of [[Myanmar]]. The [[Strait of Malacca]] separates it from [[Sumatra]], and the Straits of Johor separate its south coast from [[Singapore]]. The Titiwangsa Mountains form its backbone, and the Kra Isthmus is its narrowest point. The term *Tanah Melayu* ("Malay land") appears in texts from the early 17th century, including the *Hikayat Hang Tuah*, where it refers to the area under the [[Malacca Sultanate]]. In the early 20th century, Malay nationalists used the term to call for uniting the peninsula's Malay states, an ambition largely realized in the Federation of Malaya in 1948. The peninsula is covered with tropical moist broadleaf forests, with dipterocarp trees in the lowlands.

Dravidian language spoken mainly by the Malayali people in [[Kerala]], India. It is one of 22 scheduled languages and one of 11 classical languages of India, with official status in Kerala, [[Lakshadweep]] and Puducherry. It has about 38 million native speakers as of 2023, including large diaspora communities in the [[Persian Gulf]] countries. The mainstream view holds that it descends from a western coastal dialect of early Middle Tamil, separating from it between the 9th and 13th centuries. The oldest extant literary work in Malayalam distinct from the Tamil tradition is *Ramacharitam*, a [[Ramayana]] adaptation from the late 12th or early 13th century. Its script derives from Vatteluttu, extended with Grantha letters to write Indo-Aryan loanwords. The modern grammar is based on *Kerala Panineeyam*, written in the late 19th century.

Passenger flight that disappeared in 2014 on a route from Kuala Lumpur to [[Beijing Capital International Airport]], with 227 passengers and 12 crew aboard. The [[Boeing 777]] lost contact with [[Air traffic control|air traffic control]] over the [[South China Sea]], and military radar tracked it turning westward across the [[Malay Peninsula]]. Its cause remains undetermined. The search of the [[Indian Ocean]] cost US$135–160 million, the most expensive in aviation history, and found no main wreckage. Debris, including a flaperon found on Réunion, was confirmed as coming from the aircraft. Industry safety rules were revised afterward, including longer recording times on [[Flight recorder|flight data recorders]].

British-Canadian journalist and author. Gladwell has been a staff writer for *The New Yorker* since 1996 and has published eight books, including *The Tipping Point*, *Blink* and *Outliers*. His writing draws on research in [[Sociology]] and [[Psychology]], often through anecdote. He covered business and science for [[The Washington Post]] from 1987 to 1996 and was raised in rural [[Ontario]]. He hosts the podcast *Revisionist History*. Scholars have criticized his books for prioritizing storytelling and selective examples over rigorous empirical analysis, sometimes distorting the studies they cite. He was appointed to the Order of Canada in 2011.

English actor. Born Malcolm John Taylor, he took his professional name because another actor already had that name. He first became known for playing Mick Travis in Lindsay Anderson's *If....* (1968). [[Stanley Kubrick]] cast him as Alex in *A Clockwork Orange* (1971), the role for which he became best known. His later films include *Time After Time* (1979), *Caligula* (1979) and *Star Trek Generations* (1994). He also voiced characters in animated series and video games, such as Metallo in *Superman: The Animated Series*. He received a star on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]] in 2012.

African American Muslim minister and civil rights leader. Born Malcolm Little, he was imprisoned for larceny and burglary before joining the [[Nation of Islam]]. He served as its public face for 12 years, advocating black empowerment and separation of Black and white Americans. He criticized [[Martin Luther King Jr.]] and the mainstream [[Civil rights movement]] for their emphasis on nonviolence and integration. From the 1950s he was under surveillance by the [[Federal Bureau of Investigation]]. In the 1960s he broke with [[Elijah Muhammad]], completed the [[Hajj]] to Mecca, and embraced [[Sunni Islam]]. Critics accused him of preaching violence, while supporters credit him with advancing racial justice. He was assassinated in [[New York City]], and three Nation of Islam members were charged with the murder. Two of those convictions were vacated in 2021. His autobiography, written with Alex Haley, was published posthumously in 1965.

Island country and [[Archipelago|archipelago]] in [[South Asia]] and the [[Indian Ocean]] (pop., 2022: 515,132). Its 26 [[Atoll|atolls]] stretch across the equator, and its 298 sq km of land is spread over about 90,000 sq km of sea. Malé is the capital. The Maldives is the smallest country in Asia, and its highest natural point of 2.4 m above sea level makes it the world's lowest-lying country. Islam reached the islands in the 12th century, and the Maldives became a sultanate with ties to Asia and Africa. It became a British protectorate in 1887 and gained independence in 1965. A presidential republic was established in 1968. Tourism is now the largest sector, ahead of fishing, which was historically dominant. The Maldives is a member of the [[United Nations]] and the [[Commonwealth of Nations]], and its state religion is [[Sunni Islam]]. Its low elevation leaves it highly vulnerable to [[Climate change|rising sea levels]].

Sex of an [[Organism|organism]] that produces, or is organized to produce, [[Sperm|sperm]], the smaller gamete that fuses with the larger ovum in fertilization. A male cannot reproduce sexually without access to an ovum from a female, though some organisms reproduce both sexually and asexually. Most male mammals, including humans, have a Y chromosome that codes for higher levels of [[Testosterone]] to develop male reproductive organs. Separate sexes have evolved independently in many lineages through anisogamy, the difference in gamete size, and male gametes are also produced by chytrids, diatoms and land plants. The Mars symbol ♂ was first used to denote sex by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in 1751. In humans, *male* can also refer to [[Gender|gender]] role or gender identity.

Organs of the human male that produce and deliver [[Sperm|sperm]], located outside the body and within the pelvis. The penis and the scrotum are the main external organs. The scrotum holds the [[Testicle|testicles]], which produce sperm in the seminiferous tubules and secrete androgens. Sperm mature in the epididymis, then travel through the vas deferens, a tube about 30 cm long, to the ejaculatory duct. Three accessory glands supply fluid that lubricates the ducts and nourishes sperm: the seminal vesicles, which secrete many components of [[Semen]], the [[Prostate|prostate gland]], and the bulbourethral glands. During [[Sexual intercourse|sexual intercourse]], semen exits through the [[Urethra]], which also carries urine. The scrotum keeps the testicles about 2–3°C below core body temperature, which is needed for sperm production.

Landlocked country in [[West Africa]] (pop., 2024: 25.20 million). Its capital and largest city is [[Bamako]]. Mali covers 1,240,192 sq km, and its northern part extends deep into the Sahara. Most people live in the south, where the Niger and Senegal rivers run. Gold accounts for 80% of exports, and the economy centers on agriculture and mining. Mali was part of three successive West African empires that controlled [[Trans-Saharan trade]]: the [[Ghana Empire]], the [[Mali Empire]] and the [[Songhai Empire]]. At its peak in 1300, the Mali Empire was the wealthiest country in Africa under [[Mansa Musa]], and [[Timbuktu]] became a renowned center of learning. France seized control in the late 19th century, and Mali became independent in 1960. Military coups in 2020 and 2021 brought Assimi Goita to power, and in 2025 all political parties were dissolved.

Muslim jurist and [[Hadith|hadith]] scholar, eponym of the Maliki school of Islamic jurisprudence. Born in [[Medina]], he studied under teachers including Ja'far al-Sadiq and became the premier scholar of hadith in his day. Contemporaries called him the Imam of Medina. His legal views became normative for much of [[Sunni Islam|Sunni]] practice in [[North Africa]], [[Al-Andalus|al-Andalus]], Egypt, Syria, Yemen and Sudan. His compilation *al-Muwatta'* is one of the oldest and most revered Sunni hadith collections, and it aimed to set out law according to the consensus and sunna of Medina. [[Al-Shafi'i]] called it "the soundest book on earth after the [[Quran]]". Malik is venerated across the traditional Sunni schools, and mystics often regard him as a saint.

Dabbling duck (*Anas platyrhynchos*) of temperate and subtropical North America, [[Eurasia]] and North Africa, also called the wild duck. Drakes have green heads, while ducks are mainly brown-speckled; both sexes have a speculum of white-bordered black, purple or blue feathers on the wings. The mallard is 50–65 cm long, with a wingspan of 81–98 cm. Females lay 8 to 13 eggs, and incubation takes 27 to 28 days. Mallards live in wetlands and are adaptable enough to thrive in cities. They are the main ancestor of most domestic duck breeds and interbreed with closely related wild species, a process of [[Hybrid (biology)|hybridization]] that can threaten native waterfowl. The IUCN classifies the species as least concern. It has been introduced to the [[Falkland Islands]], New Zealand and Australia, and is considered an [[Invasive species]] in some regions.

Largest island in the [[Balearic Islands]] of Spain, and the seventh-largest in the [[Mediterranean Sea]]. Also spelled Majorca in English, its name derives from Latin *insula maior* ("larger island"). Settlement began in the 3rd millennium BC, and the Talaiotic culture raised [[Bronze Age]] megaliths. [[Phoenicia|Phoenician]] colonies followed from the 8th century BC, and the island later passed to [[Carthage]] and then Rome. [[Tourism]] accounts for about 75% of output, and Palma de Mallorca Airport handled 28 million passengers in 2017.

Health condition caused by too few or too many nutrients, or an imbalance among them. Malnutrition includes undernutrition, which can cause stunting, wasting and being underweight, and overnutrition, which can cause [[Obesity]] and toxic levels of micronutrients. Undernutrition causes the highest mortality rate in children, particularly those under 5. Micronutrient deficiencies, most commonly of [[Iodine]], [[Vitamin|vitamin A]] and iron, affect half of children under 5 and two-thirds of women of reproductive age worldwide. [[Anemia]] is most often caused by iron deficiency. The [[World Health Organization]] describes a "double burden of malnutrition" in which overnutrition and undernutrition coexist. Up to 40% of hospitalized patients are estimated to have disease-related malnutrition.

Island country in the central [[Mediterranean Sea]] (pop., 2024: 574,250), consisting of Malta, Gozo and Comino. Its capital is [[Valletta]]. Inhabited since at least 6500 BC, Malta was ruled by Phoenicians, Carthaginians, Romans, Arabs, Normans and the [[Knights Hospitaller]], who held the islands for 268 years from 1530. It came under British rule as a crown colony in the early 19th century and endured Axis bombing in [[World War II]], for which it was awarded the George Cross. Malta gained independence in 1964 and became a republic in 1974. It joined the [[European Union]] in 2004 and adopted the [[Euro]] in 2008. It is a member of the [[Commonwealth of Nations]] and the United Nations. Catholicism is the [[State religion|state religion]], and the economy is now high-income, driven by tourism, financial services and manufacturing.

Archipelago in eastern [[Indonesia]], also known as the Moluccas. The islands were called the Spice Islands because [[Nutmeg|nutmeg]], mace and [[Clove|cloves]] grew only there, which drew European colonial interest in the 16th century. Arab merchants brought [[Islam]] in the 14th century, while aboriginal animism persisted in the hinterlands. The [[Dutch East India Company]] came to dominate the region in the 17th century. During the Dutch–Portuguese War, also called the Spice War, many island populations, especially in the Banda Islands, were massacred. The islands formed a single province from Indonesian independence until 1999, when they were split in two. North Maluku is predominantly Muslim, while Maluku province has a larger [[Christianity|Christian]] population.

Family of [[Flowering plant|flowering plants]], commonly called the mallows. It contains an estimated 244 genera with 4225 known species, ranging from herbs to [[Shrub|shrubs]] and [[Tree|trees]]. Economically important members include cacao, cola, [[Cotton|cotton]], [[Okra|okra]], roselle and [[Durian|durian]]. Ornamental genera include *Alcea* (hollyhock), *Malva* (mallow) and [[Tilia]] (lime or linden). Among the largest genera, *Hibiscus* has 434 species. The family's boundaries are debated; a broad circumscription adds the families Bombacaceae, Tiliaceae and Sterculiaceae, which genetic studies showed are not monophyletic. Some members, such as the kapok tree, yield timber and stuffing materials, and cotton supplies textile fiber. The family is found on every continent except Antarctica.

Malicious software intentionally designed to disrupt or damage a [[Computer]], server or network, leak private information or gain unauthorized access to systems. Researchers classify malware into types including [[Virus|computer viruses]], worms, [[Trojan Horse|Trojan horses]], ransomware, spyware and keyloggers. [[John von Neumann]] showed in theory that a program could reproduce itself. Fred Cohen experimented with viruses, and his 1987 doctoral dissertation was on the subject. Early computer viruses spread by infecting programs or the boot sectors of [[Floppy disk|floppy disks]] and were written for the [[Apple II]] and Mac. The first IBM PC virus in the wild, a boot sector virus called (c)Brain, appeared in 1986. The first well-known worm, the Morris worm of 1988, exploited security holes in [[Unix]] systems to spread. Defenses include antivirus software, firewalls, regular patches and backups. Ransomware alone was projected to cost $57 billion globally in 2025.

Genus of fast-moving, highly venomous snakes, *Dendroaspis*, in the family Elapidae. Its name means "tree asp" in Greek. Four species are recognized: the [[Black mamba]], the eastern and western green mambas and Jameson's mamba. The three green species are arboreal, while the black mamba is largely terrestrial and brown or grey. All are native to [[Sub-Saharan Africa]], where they hunt birds, lizards and small mammals during the day. All mambas have medically significant [[Venom|venom]], and the [[World Health Organization]] classifies them as snakes of medical importance. The black mamba, Africa's longest venomous snake, reaches up to 14 feet. Its venom causes paralysis and respiratory or cardiac failure if untreated, but antivenom is available. Mambas generally avoid contact with humans and usually escape threats by speed.

Slave-soldier or enslaved mercenary in the Muslim world. Mamluks were purchased as military slaves, converted to Islam and trained in warfare. After training they were freed but remained in the ruling military caste, forming elite regiments that in some periods rose to sovereign power. The institution developed under the [[Abbasid Caliphate]] in the 9th century and spread to include Circassians, Mongols, Georgians and Armenians. Mamluk factions seized the sultanate centered on [[Egypt]] and [[Syria]] in 1250. The [[Mamluk Sultanate]] defeated the Mongol [[Ilkhanate]] at Ain Jalut in 1260 and expelled the last [[Crusades|Crusaders]] from the [[Levant]] in 1302. In Egypt, Mamluks held status above the general population until their massacre by Muhammad Ali in 1811.

State in Egypt, the [[Levant]] and the Hejaz (1250–1517), with [[Cairo]] as its capital. It was ruled by a military caste of mamluks, freed slave-soldiers, headed by a sultan. The sultanate was established in 1250 with the overthrow of the Ayyubid dynasty. Under sultans [[Baybars]] and Qalawun, the Mamluks defeated the [[Mongols]] in 1260 and conquered the [[Crusader states]] by the end of the 13th century. They then expanded into Nubia, Cyrenaica, the Hejaz and southern Anatolia. Internal strife and financial distress weakened the sultanate under later rulers. In 1516, Qansuh al-Ghuri was killed in battle against the [[Ottoman Empire|Ottoman]] sultan [[Selim I]], who conquered Egypt in 1517 and ended Mamluk rule. Cairo was one of the largest cities in the world at the time, and Mamluk architecture still makes up much of its historic fabric.
